title: Investigate the possibilities of establishing and running a small business enterprise (SMME)

lessons.title: SMMEs and finding a business opportunity
lessons.html:
What is an SMME?

SMME stands for small, medium and micro enterprise. In South Africa SMMEs range from a one-person spaza or a backyard vegetable seller (micro) to a family packhouse or transport business with dozens of workers (small and medium). Together they create a large share of jobs, especially in rural areas. Government defines size categories for SMMEs by sector, using turnover thresholds, and these are used to decide who qualifies for certain support.

Why start your own business?

  • Earn an income and create jobs for others in your community.
  • Use your skills and knowledge, for example in fruit handling or farming.
  • Be independent and build something for your family.

But running a business also means risk: income is not guaranteed, you may work long hours and you can lose the money you invest.

Finding business opportunities around the farm and packhouse

Look for needs that are not being met. Examples in the perishable produce industry include:

  • supplying packaging materials or pallets to packhouses;
  • transport services for bins and pallets;
  • contract labour services for harvesting, with proper labour compliance;
  • cleaning or pest control services for packhouses;
  • processing fruit that does not make export grade;
  • a farm stall or local delivery of fresh produce;
  • nursery plants, seedlings or compost.

Personal assessment

Before starting, ask yourself honestly:

  • Do I have the skills to produce the product or service?
  • Can I sell, keep records and manage money?
  • Do I have the time, health and family support?
  • How much money can I put in, and how much can I afford to lose?

Successful entrepreneurs are usually persistent, willing to learn, good at solving problems and careful with money.

lessons.title: Setting up and running the SMME
lessons.html:
Investigating whether the business can work

Do a simple feasibility study before committing:

  1. Market: who will buy, how much, how often and at what price? Talk to at least ten possible customers.
  2. Competition: who else offers this, and how will you be different?
  3. Resources: premises, equipment, vehicles, workers and suppliers.
  4. Money: start-up costs, monthly running costs and expected income.
  5. Legal: registration, licences and compliance.

Legal forms and registration

  • Sole proprietor: simple, but the owner is personally liable for debts.
  • Partnership: two or more owners share profit and liability.
  • Private company (Pty) Ltd: registered with the Companies and Intellectual Property Commission (CIPC); a separate legal person.
  • Co-operative: owned by members, common among small farmers.

Register for tax with SARS, and if you employ workers register for UIF and follow labour laws, including minimum wages and safe working conditions under the OHS Act 85 of 1993.

Sources of support and finance

  • Own savings and family.
  • Banks and the Land Bank for agricultural loans.
  • Government development agencies, such as the Small Enterprise Development and Finance Agency (SEDFA), and provincial departments of agriculture.
  • Mentorship from commercial farmers, industry associations and enterprise development programmes.

Running the business day to day

  • Keep separate bank accounts for business and personal money.
  • Record all income and expenses daily.
  • Issue invoices and follow up on payments.
  • Look after customers and deliver on promises.
  • Plan for the seasons: save in good months for the quiet months.
  • Review results monthly and adjust.

Key points

  • SMMEs range from micro to medium enterprises and create many jobs.
  • Look for unmet needs in your local industry.
  • Assess yourself and the opportunity honestly before starting.
  • Choose a legal form and register with CIPC, SARS and UIF as needed.
  • Separate business and personal money and keep daily records.
